title: Three providers: apps, plans, and features

opening.headline: We cover how to read names by dividing them into five layers when companies, models, products, features, and plans are mixed in one sentence.
body: When you hear about AI tools, you come across sentences like, ‘On the Pro plan, just turn on Sol and run Deep Research.’ This one sentence contains the name of the product, plan, model, and feature. If you don't know which floor you're talking about, you won't be able to determine whether you should upgrade your plan, change models, or turn on features.

In this lesson, we divide the name into five layers: company, model, product (chat app), features, and plan. Next, we read the plan systems of the three products ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini in the same framework, and compare how the individual plan and team plan differ in terms of functionality and management. After looking at representative functions such as file upload, file creation, artifacts, and personalization, we solve the single need of document summarization layer by layer.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: You can distinguish between companies, models, products, functions, and plans.
You can compare the features and management differences between individual, team, and corporate plans.

screens.title: If the names are mixed up, you don't know what's what.
screens.lead: This is a message from a colleague posted on the company messenger. Select the underlined phrases in the sentences below to see which layer they are named for.

visual.alt: A scene where a colleague's one-sentence message is posted on the company messenger screen, and each word is underlined in a different color.
labels: Just turn on Sol on the Pro plan and run Deep Research.

data.text: Colleague's message: Choose GPT-6.1 Sol model from ChatGPT to Pro plan, turn on Deep Research Features, and start it. This one sentence includes OpenAI's product ChatGPT, the subscription-based model Pro plan, the reasoning engine GPT-6.1 Sol model, and the tool embedded in the app Deep Research Features all at once.

marks.note: This is the product layer. It is a chat app that users open and was created by a company called OpenAI. The app name is different from the model name.
This is the plan floor. It is a subscription unit that determines usage, available functions, and management scope. Upgrading a plan is different from changing the model.
This is the model layer. This is the engine that actually creates the answer within the app. ChatGPT help explains that paid plans offer several entry-level models to choose from.
This is the functional layer. This is a tool provided by the app that reads and synthesizes multiple online sources to produce structured results with citations.

screens.outro: We confirmed that one sentence is divided into four layers. Now let’s think about the AI ​​app you use.

screens.title: Think about the AI apps you use
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Can you tell the difference between the name of the AI app you are currently using and the name of the model used within it?
items.answer: The app name and model name are often used interchangeably. But ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini apps are products that users open, and the model is the engine that creates the answers within them. You need to distinguish between the two so you can decide whether to change the app or model.

items.prompt: Have you ever heard, ‘This feature is only available on paid plans’?
items.answer: Even within the same app, the available functions and models vary depending on the plan. ChatGPT help explains that built-in tools may be available depending on your subscription level and settings. So, before saying ‘yes or no’, you must first check which plan you are talking about.

items.prompt: If you have ever uploaded a file or received a result, which app was it from?
items.answer: Methods and limits for uploading files and creating results vary from app to app. If you write down which app and plan you had the experience you just remembered, it will be directly linked to the explanation of the function layer on the following screen.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized our experience, let's build a five-layer framework to divide the names.

screens.title: Five layers: Company, Model, Product, Feature, Plan
screens.lead: Select the arrows to move through each level and see the five levels stack up from the bottom. Each layer is accompanied by examples from three companies.

visual.alt: A schematic of five layers of company, model, product, feature, and plan stacked vertically, each layer labeled with examples of the three companies.

steps.title: 1st floor company
steps.body: At the bottom is the company. These include OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. Companies make models and products, but you can't tell which model or app they're talking about just by looking at the company name.

steps.title: 2nd floor model
steps.body: A model is the engine that creates answers within the app. Examples include GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon. ChatGPT help explains that users on paid plans can choose from several basic models. Even if the model name changes, the app name may remain the same.

steps.title: Third-tier product (chat app)
steps.body: The product is a chat app that users open directly. These include ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini apps. Even if it is a model from the same company, how it is provided within the app varies depending on the product. At work, the first clue is which apps you already have an account with.

steps.title: 4th floor function
steps.body: Features are tools that apps put on top of models. Representative examples include web search, deep research, image input and creation, file upload, data analysis, canvas, memory, and projects. ChatGPT help explains that these built-in tools are available depending on your subscription level and settings.

steps.title: 5th floor plan
steps.body: A plan is a subscription unit that determines usage, features, and management scope, such as Free, Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise. Even if it has the same model name, available functions may vary depending on the product and plan. So, when you hear the word ‘you can do it’, you need to get into the habit of asking which product and which plan it is.

screens.outro: Now that we've covered the five levels, let's compare how the three companies' tips break down the plans.

screens.title: Structure and plan system of the three companies’ help
screens.lead: Select each tab to see how the three products describe their features and plans. The last tab organizes the common framework for reading the plan table.

tabs.label: ChatGPT
tabs.body:
The 'Function Overview' document in ChatGPT Help introduces search (web navigation), deep research, image input and creation, file and audio upload, data analysis, voice mode, Canvas, memory, and projects in one place. These tools are available depending on your subscription level and settings.

What is noteworthy in this document is the explanation that users with paid plans can choose from several basic models, and the comment that memory cannot be used in a custom GPT. Model releases, feature changes, and discontinuation notices are gathered in one place in separate model release notes.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body:
Claude's fee information is divided into Free, Pro, and Max. Free also includes web browsing, file creation, code execution, cross-conversation memory, app linking, and Artifacts. In addition to Free, Pro offers more usage, task scheduling, Claude Code, more Claude models, and Claude in Chrome integration with Microsoft 365. Max offers 5x or 20x the usage of Pro, has higher output limits and priority access during peak times.

Team and Enterprise are organizational plans that include security and management features such as central billing, single sign-on, and role-based access.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body:
In Gemini's subscription instructions, Free includes Flash-Lite model access, image creation and editing, Deep Research, Gemini Live, Canvas, and Gems. Google AI Plus boasts the same features as Free, plus access to the Flash model and twice the usage limits of Free. Above that there are Pro and Ultra tiers, and the Pro and Ultra guide pages introduce Gemini 4 Argon access.

Gemini app help provides separate explanations for each function, such as Canvas, View Related Sources, and Gemini Live. So, you should read the plan table and function help together.

tabs.label: common reading framework
tabs.body:
The plan table can be read in four rows to compare the three products in the same way. The first is usage, which is how much of the same function can be used. The second is model selection, which model you approach. Third is functionality: whether it includes search, deep research, or file processing. Fourth is management tools: whether there is central billing or rights management.

Even with different plans, the chat screen may look pretty much the same. Don't judge whether the same function exists just by looking at the screen; check the plan table and help separately to see if the function exists.

screens.outro: Now that we have seen the big picture of the plan, let’s compare in detail how the individual plan and team plan differ.

screens.title: Differences in functions and management between individual, team, and corporate plans
screens.lead: Each row in the table shows where the Personal and Team plans differ. Read from top to bottom to find out what's added in terms of management.

data.caption: Claude's Personal Plan vs. Team Plan
rows: It increases as you go from Free to Pro and Max, and Max is 5 or 20 times higher than Pro.
It offers a larger per-session usage limit than Pro, and you can purchase usage credits in advance and use them beyond the limit.
Individuals make and manage their own payments
Manage member access and payments in one place with admin tools and central billing
Log in with your personal account
Provides single sign-on (SSO), domain capture, just-in-time provisioning, and role-based permissions.
Spending limits can be set on an organizational and individual basis
Provides connectors for business tools such as Google Drive, Gmail, Google Calendar, GitHub, Microsoft 365, and Slack, as well as organizational search projects.
It's on by default, but org owners can turn it off in org settings.
data.notes: The Enterprise plan also has code execution and file creation turned on by default in new organizations and can be turned off by owners. Network access is turned off by default, but owners can turn it on and even whitelist domains. To summarize, the personal plan is based on individual usage, and the team and enterprise plans are based on management, security, and sharing scope. The most important difference is that even if the plan name is the same, the features available to each employee may vary depending on the organization owner's settings. So, if an employee says 'I can't do it', the first order is to check the organization settings before changing the model or app. Since you cannot change whether the feature is turned off unless you are an administrator, it is also a good idea to know the route to request from the administrator.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized the plan layer, let's look at the file and output functions, which are representative examples of the functional layer.

screens.title: Functional Layer: File Upload, File Creation, Artifacts, Personalization
screens.lead: When you select a card, it flips over and a description appears. Select the right arrow to advance to the next card and discover the four signature features.

visual.alt: Four icon cards representing File Upload, File Creation, Artifacts, and Personalization.

cards.back: Claude can upload documents such as PDF, DOCX, CSV, TXT, and HTML as well as JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP images. Upload up to 20 files per chat, up to 500MB per file. If the PDF is less than 100 pages, text, pictures, and charts are analyzed. If the PDF is less than 100 pages, only the text is processed. If it exceeds 1000 pages, it cannot be uploaded. Project files can be up to 30MB per file.

Claude runs the code to create and download Excel, PowerPoint, Word, and PDF files. Code execution and file creation are available in Free, Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise, and in Team and Enterprise, organization owners can turn them off in the settings. Therefore, even with the same request, results may vary from person to person.

Artifacts are the results you display to others, such as designs, slides, documents, dashboards, and small interactive tools. It opens next to the conversation so you can edit it and come back to view and share it. You can create from any plan, or start from document, slide, and design templates. Dashboard templates are in beta and available on Pro and higher plans.

Gemini's Canvas and Gems, Claude's memory and user preferences, and ChatGPT's memory and projects are features that help you use the app to suit you. ChatGPT Help explains that when you turn on Memory, it will remember information like your name, preferences, and goals to personalize future answers, and you can view, edit, or delete what you remember at any time.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the functional layers, let's break down the actual needs by layer.

screens.title: Case Commentary 1: A document summary is needed
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down one request into five layers. Select the arrows to follow what you see in what order.

steps.title: request
steps.body: The case is like this: At work, I'm given a 50-page PDF report and need to summarize just the main points. You'll often start looking for the model name in this one line, but there's another layer to check first.

steps.title: product layer
steps.body: Among ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, look first at the apps you already have a work account with. This is because introducing a new app requires a separate account and security review. If you already have an app that can solve your need, it's easier to get started with that app.

steps.title: functional layer
steps.body: Here are the features: Check whether the file can be uploaded and, even if so, what the page limit is. Claude analyzes both text and visual elements in PDFs under 100 pages, so a 50-page report can be summarized with pictures and charts included. If it exceeds 100 pages, only the text will be processed.

steps.title: Plan floor
steps.body: See if the free plan is enough. If your usage is limited, you may need a higher plan. If you're on a Team plan, also check to see if your administrator has turned off features like running code and creating files. Cases where a colleague is on the same plan but you are not are usually resolved at this point.

steps.title: model floor
steps.body: Lastly, the model. If it is a long document, it is viewed based on the context limit. The longer the document, the more the input takes up the window, so make sure the model has enough space to hold the summary results. The model is judged last among the layers. This is because the candidates have already been narrowed down in the previous floor. If you check in this order, if you can't summarize, you can immediately pinpoint which floor you're stuck on.

screens.outro: Now that we have solved one summary, let's see how the number of layers to be checked increases as the results and sharing are added.

screens.title: Case commentary 2: When the summary includes results and team sharing
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to compare how the floors you inspect change as demand increases.

states.label: Summary only
states.body:
If the only request is 'summarize a 50-page PDF', the layers to check are short. At the product layer, you determine which apps you have an account for, and at the feature layer, you check PDF uploads and page limits. At your plan tier, check to see if the usage you need is within the free limits.

In this case, the result is enough as a text on the chat screen, so file creation, sharing functions, or administrator settings are not required. The smaller the request, the fewer layers to check. In other words, you can estimate the scope of inspection in advance by writing down the request in one line and checking whether it includes a result format or a sharing target. Deciding the scope first like this reduces unnecessary checking. This case is the first state, where the floor inspection is the shortest.

states.label: Summary + Slides + Share
states.body:
If there is a request to create a slide and share the summary results with the team, the number of layers to check increases.

First we need to create a file in the functional layer. Claude lets you create PowerPoint files by running code, or you can get started with Artifacts' Slides template.

Next, the plan tier changes. The scope of sharing and collaboration features varies by plan, so you should check whether your current plan covers them.

Finally, the management layer comes into play. On Team and Enterprise plans, owners can turn off code execution and file creation, so if that doesn't work, you'll need to check with your administrator for settings.

In conclusion, as your needs grow, there are more layers to check in that order: features, plans, and management settings.

screens.outro: Now that we've finished the case, let's summarize the main points of this lesson.

screens.title: Organizing questions into five layers
screens.lead: Summarize how the five-layer framework created in this class solves the first sentence.

paragraphs: Read the first sentence again, ‘On the Pro plan, just turn on Sol and run Deep Research.’ Now we can see that this sentence refers to three conditions at once: plan layer (Pro), model layer (Sol), and function layer (Deep Research). If one is missing, the results will not be the same.

The five layers answer different questions. The company and model tell you who made what engine, the product tells you which app you open, the features tell you what the app can do, and the plan tells you how much you spend and who manages it.

When encountering a new name, first ask which floor it is from. And when it gets clogged, check the layers from bottom to top. Remember that Team and Enterprise plans have an extra layer called Admin Settings.

callout.label: standards to remember
callout.text: When you hear the word ‘you can do it’, ask which product plan it is for and what features it has.

glossary.def: This is the product screen that the user opens directly. These include ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini apps.
A subscription unit that determines usage, functionality, and management scope. There are Free, Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise, etc.
This is an official guidance document that gathers information on model releases, feature changes, and discontinuation in one place.
The output feature opens next to the conversation so you can edit and share it. You can create documents, slides, designs, dashboards, and more.
This feature allows the app to reflect the user's preferences or memories in the answer. Examples include memory or user preferences.

misconceptions.myth: The model name and product name are the same thing.
misconceptions.fact: A model is an engine that creates answers, and a product is an app that contains that engine. Even if the app name remains the same, the model inside may be different.

misconceptions.myth: If the plan is the same, all features are the same.
misconceptions.fact: Team and Enterprise plans allow org owners to turn features like running code and creating files on or off. Even within the same plan, features vary depending on the organization’s settings.

misconceptions.myth: Any model can be used as long as it is a paid plan.
misconceptions.fact: Available models and features vary depending on the product and plan. Just because you can choose from multiple models on a paid plan doesn't mean you'll use all of them.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Company, Model, Product, Feature, Plan are names of different layers.
The chat app is the product, the model is the engine within it, and the plan determines usage, features, and management scope.
Uploading and creating files, Artifacts, and personalization are features affected by your plan and management settings.
As your needs grow, there are more layers to check in that order: features, plans, and management settings.
